Blood sweat and expropriation: The Fight for Farmland in Georgia

By: Nickolaus Bauer | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
Exclusive follow up by South African media on the South African farming community in Georgia since its beginnings 15 years ago

Summary:
For nearly two decades, a community of South African farmers has carved out a life in the fertile valleys of the Republic of Georgia — a land once scarred by Soviet rule, now transformed into an unlikely home for expat agriculturalists. But the same soil that once offered new hope is now the site of rising tension, quiet dispossession, and shifting legal sands.
New restrictions on foreign ownership of agricultural land, coupled with state interference in production rights, have left some farmers thriving — and others stripped of everything they’ve built. As Georgia tightens its grip on food sovereignty, Carte Blanche travels to the Caucasus to uncover the untold story of South African farmers who say they were welcomed in, only to be quietly pushed out.
This story explores the rise, fall, and uncertain future of a pioneering community, caught between geopolitics, legal grey zones, and the unrelenting demands of survival.




Further information:
Key Themes:
The Dream:
South Africans began arriving in Georgia in the early 2010s, drawn by arable land and promises of opportunity
Community efforts led to commercial farms producing beef, vegetables and supporting food security in Georgia
Initial government support and community acceptance
The Shift:
Recent laws prohibit foreign ownership of agricultural land without special government dispensation
Some farmers have kept their land under complex leases or local proxies
Others claim the state used water permits, sales blockades, and licensing bureaucracy to force them off
The Fallout:
Former farmers like Schalk Krüger describe a slow-motion “expropriation”
Rising mistrust and refusal by most expats to speak publicly
Growing sense of betrayal and legal limbo
Tensions between Georgia’s national food strategy and individual farmers’ rights
The Broader Landscape:
Georgia’s positioning as a low-tax haven and crypto-friendly hub
Growing South African presence not just in agriculture, but tech, medicine and financial services
Mixed messages from the Georgian state — pro-investment but increasingly protectionist
Echoes of South Africa’s own land reform debates playing out in reverse

Visual Approach:
Cinematic Rural Georgia: Drone shots of fertile farmland, machinery, and homesteads in contrast with abandoned fields and government-seized properties
Testimony and Tension: Walk-and-talk interviews with farmers on their land (and those who’ve lost it), showing subtle fear, resilience, and resignation
Documents and Data: Legal graphics outlining changes in Georgian agricultural law; satellite imagery of seized land; maps of Georgian-South African farming zones
Contrast and Context: Scenes from Tbilisi’s crypto and forex hubs juxtaposed with remote, embattled farmsteads
Emotional Layer: Intimate reflections on community, betrayal, and what it means to start again — only to be uprooted twice

Extra Budget Items:
3 days camera operator @ $1300 including full kit

3 nights accommodation in Georgia

R E P O R T A G E
Blood, Sweat and the Fight for Land in Georgia
For nearly two decades, a community of South African farmers has carved out a life in the Republic of Georgia, drawn by arable land and promises of opportunity. They were followed by a growing South African presence in tech, medicine and financial services. But the same soil that once offered new hope is now the site of rising tension. In the face of new restrictions on foreign land ownership, state interference and red tape, farmers are leaving the land they helped develop. Carte Blanche speaks to the South African farmers who say they were welcomed in, only to be quietly pushed out.
Producer & Presenter: Nickolaus Bauer

Script:



(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Agriculture brought into the 21st century through South African blood and sweat.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
15 years ago, a group of South African farmers was lured to Georgia - a former soviet state in Eastern Europe

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
On the promise of a bright future and a place in the sun.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
But these pioneers aren’t as welcome as they once were.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Georgia is a tiny nation between Eastern Europe and Western Asia. Historically, it’s been a net importer of food, meaning it’s never been able to produce enough to feed its 3.7 million people.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
So, in 2011, the government began an aggressive campaign to recruit South African farmers.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
They had an ambitious goal: to raise the contribution of agriculture to the Georgian economy from 5% to 20% in just ten years.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Critically, skills would have to be transferred to locals. PAUSE Around fifty South African farmers took up the offer.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
At the time, Georgia was on the march to become a more liberalised and open economy, with hopes of joining the European Union.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Schalk Kruger, from Marble Hall in Limpopo, was one of the first to arrive. He farmed wheat and maize in a region called Gardabani, about 35 kilometers from the capital, Tbilisi.

(SCHALK KRUGER)
I saw something here, you know, and then we bought this farm from a Georgian company, and we brought our first irrigation systems and tractors from South Africa to here. And we start farming.


(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
The earth was barren and the farming culture was stuck in outdated, inefficient methods. But Schalk and his partners painstakingly built up the land, installing Georgia’s very first pivot irrigation system - a mechanised sprinkler that waters large fields efficiently.

In just two years, they transformed hundreds of hectares of fallow land into productive fields…sharing their knowledge along the way.

(SCHALK KRUGER)
Actually, Georgians are very, very quick learners. And the moment we we start developed with daai centre pivot opsit, die volgende jaar dan begin julle pivots ook opsit me and the government give them cheap loans

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Things were looking up…. but only briefly. After just five years, Schalk threw in the towel, frustrated by clashes with neighbours over water and grazing rights and the rising costs of farming.

(SCHALK KRUGER)
We planted 200 hectares and we think we will pay for 200 hectares of water. No, we’ve got 1000 hectares. We must pay for a 1000 hectares of water. We must pay for a 1000 hectares of land tax. Even if we not use it and let that is 250,000. Every year there's more than a million rand a year that we didn’t bargain on. So we ran out of cash.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Schalk sold for a small profit and moved on. The land he developed is now in Georgian hands.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
It’s a common story among the South Africans farming here. Some, like Schalk, sold their farms and stayed in Georgia. Many returned home.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
This farm was built up using South African expertise. Some of these very farming implements and equipment being imported from there into Georgia. Its success hinging on the support given by the first generation of South African farmers that immigrated here almost 15 years ago.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Leven Akhvledini is here largely thanks to the South Africans. A lawyer by training, he’s spent the past decade farming. He’s one of several Georgian professionals moving into agriculture off the back of South African skills.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
His 110-hectare farm in a place called Sartichala produces 14 tonnes of maize per hectare.



(LEVEN AKHVLEDINI)
This idea of, South Africans to Georgia. I think it was successful because this focal point, what we did here is spread around and we show this success story to the neighbours, to the all the other regions and Georgians, farmers, and they start following. And, you know, they copy, copy, paste us

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Leven and many other novice Georgian farmers have learned the ins and outs from Piet Kemp, a farmer from Heilbron in the Free State.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
He’s currently overseeing thousands of hectares down the road from Leven, producing wheat, corn and cattle for a Georgian consortium.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)

He says there was almost nothing here when he first arrived

(PIET KEMP)
The problems, think I got was in the beginning to get the infrastructure there. And I think is is now really in place.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Some people call you the South African godfather of farming in Georgia. What do you think about that?

(PIET KEMP)
No, I'm just a small farmer who try to help this people. And I can see what is the challenge here. And I try to take on the challenges.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Oom Piet is in his eighties and still going strong, but he doesn’t own the land he works.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Aren’t you bitter at all now that I mean, you're 81 years of age. You've spent 15 years, good years, farming in Georgia, and you still don't own your own farm?

(PIET KEMP)
No, I love this farm. All the farms here. I'm looking for the same as my own from South Africa.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
In 2017 the Georgian government delivered a sucker punch to the South Africans farmers who’d stuck it out; making it illegal for foreigners to own agricultural land.

NICKOLAUS BAUER
Did it become more difficult when they changed the law?
PIET KEMP
I think so I'm a little bit worried about it, but I don't talk about it.

NICKOLAUS BAUER
Piet was the very first South African farmer to come to Georgia 15 years ago. But with the change in agricultural laws and the growth and competitiveness of the industry, it's doubtful any more will come soon. And with numbers dwindling, the story of South African farming in this Eastern European state might be coming to an end.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Georgia is a very different place to what Piet and the other first South African farmers encountered.

The current government is turning away from the West, and no longer eager to open the economy to foreign investment.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Now, it’s a place of arbitrary arrests…

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
…protests and a crackdown on media freedom.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
It’s a tense atmosphere we experienced, too. When we tried to speak to protesters at the Georgian parliament, our photos were taken, and we were ordered to leave.



(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Hardly an ideal environment for foreigners from the tip of Africa who just want to farm.

But Leven insists politics isn’t why South African farming in Georgia is declining.

NICKOLAUS BAUER
Why do you think that there aren't that many South African farmers still farming in Georgia, though?

(LEVEN AKHVLEDINI)
I think it is cultural misunderstanding also sometimes. (I think it is cultural misunderstanding also sometimes.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Whatever the reason, there are just a handful of South African farmers still in business here. Some are even being subsidized by their operations back home.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Charles Melville, from Addo in the Eastern Cape, and is one of the few South Africans still active in Georgia on his own land.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
It hasn’t been easy.

CHARLES MELVILLE
Pioneers get shot at. So we were pioneers and we got shot at.


(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Charles doesn’t believe the incentives that brought South Africans farmers here were genuine.

(CHARLES MELVILLE)

All of us didn't do our homework properly. And in the beginning we were sort of lied to how easy it was to acquire the land, how badly they needed us. But the government wasn't even aware of what was required. For instance, they'd say, take that piece of land in some Georgian would crawl out, the woodwork, and then you'd say, hang on, hang on. I've got a piece of paper for this from Russian Times. Luckily, I had, a fair sized fortune when I left South Africa. It's now a small fortune,

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
He’s also struggled to maintain his property rights.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
The Georgian government tried to block the transfer of land he bought before the ownership law changed in 2017 and only processed the transaction when he took them to court.

(CHARLES MELVILLE)

Many countries make it difficult for foreigners to own agricultural land. I think the safest for any foreign is to not getting involved in local politics. You've actually got nothing to do with the local politics. Leave it to the locals to sort out.


(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
So you're not worried that government may in the future change the laws and take your land away from you?

(CHARLES MELVILLE)
No, not at all. Because, If they did that, then the rule of law would also be gone in Georgia,

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Charles has decided to keep his head down, hoping to develop the local beef industry with several hundred cattle.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
We asked the Georgian government about their stance on South African farmers and foreign land ownership, but they didn’t respond.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Agriculture now makes up 7% of the Georgian economy and the country is still importing more food than it produces.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Many South Africans have returned home, but not everybody is in a hurry to leave. Even if they aren’t farming anymore.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Schalk has settled in Tbilisi with his Georgian wife Ekatarina.
EKATARINA KRUGER
We joking sometimes. I say you especially come for me, not to become farmer. Maybe because to find me.

(SCHALK KRUGER)
I don't want to go back. I'm happy here. No, no, for me. I will not get back. I. I find my happiness here, and I will stay. Yeah.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
So would you say Georgia's your home now?

(SCHALK KRUGER)
Ya! Ya!

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Oom, you asked for some Bovril so I brought you some all the way from South Africa.

(SCHALK KRUGER)
Look dear! You know what’s this?

(EKATARINA KRUGER)
Of course!

(SCHALK KRUGER)
Black gold! Jirre! Lekker!

(SCHALK KRUGER)
Bovril and Georgian khachapuri loop mooi saam!

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
IS dit jou ontbyt? (Is that your breakfast?)

(SCHALK KRUGER)
Nie onbyt! Aandete! Enige tyd van die dae!


END



PROMO 1
15 years ago, a group of South African farmers immigrated to Georgia with the hopes of starting a new life and developing the country's agricultural sector. But within a growing environment of political repression and shifting laws, numbers are dwindling and some have left the land they helped grow. Catch the full story on Carte Blanche. This Sunday.

PROMO 2
VOICEOVER:
15 years after being Invited here by the government, the promise of a better tomorrow turned out to be empty.
BYTE (CHARLES MELVILLE):
“I think naive. And the main thing is don't do their homework, but difficult to do your homework in Georgia because theare no stats and you don't understand the language. .”
VOICEOVER:
What happened to the South African farmers that trekked to the crossroads of Europe and Asia?

PROMO 3
VOICEOVER:
They gave their all— reviving the agricultural sector and growing hope…
BYTE (SCHALK KRUGER):
“For somebody who will want to resettle, sold his farm in Africa. Come here, put everything in the suitcases and come here and start forming. No, you will not. But you won't make it. You wont make it.”
VOICEOVER:
Why did the majority of South African farmers that came to Georgia leave their land?

PROMO 4
VOICEOVER:
They were once hailed as saviours of Eastern European agriculture…Now, there’s hardly any left.
BYTE (CHARLES MELVILLE):
“Georgians are xenophobic. And they are very protective of the country. When you ask them, what is all this about? They say, what else do we have? So they will try and protect their own.”
VOICEOVER:
South African farmers are fighting for survival in Georgia.

Release: R E P O R T A G E Blood, Sweat and the Fight for Land in Georgia For nearly two decades, a community of South African farmers has carved out a life in the Republic of Georgia, drawn by arable land and promises of opportunity. They were followed by a growing South African presence in tech, medicine and financial services. But the same soil that once offered new hope is now the site of rising tension. In the face of new restrictions on foreign land ownership, state interference and red tape, farmers are leaving the land they helped develop. Carte Blanche speaks to the South African farmers who say they were welcomed in, only to be quietly pushed out. Producer & Presenter: Nickolaus Bauer Script: (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Agriculture brought into the 21st century through South African blood and sweat. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) 15 years ago, a group of South African farmers was lured to Georgia - a former soviet state in Eastern Europe (NICKOLAUS BAUER) On the promise of a bright future and a place in the sun. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) But these pioneers aren’t as welcome as they once were. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Georgia is a tiny nation between Eastern Europe and Western Asia. Historically, it’s been a net importer of food, meaning it’s never been able to produce enough to feed its 3.7 million people. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) So, in 2011, the government began an aggressive campaign to recruit South African farmers. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) They had an ambitious goal: to raise the contribution of agriculture to the Georgian economy from 5% to 20% in just ten years. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Critically, skills would have to be transferred to locals. PAUSE Around fifty South African farmers took up the offer. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) At the time, Georgia was on the march to become a more liberalised and open economy, with hopes of joining the European Union. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Schalk Kruger, from Marble Hall in Limpopo, was one of the first to arrive. He farmed wheat and maize in a region called Gardabani, about 35 kilometers from the capital, Tbilisi. (SCHALK KRUGER) I saw something here, you know, and then we bought this farm from a Georgian company, and we brought our first irrigation systems and tractors from South Africa to here. And we start farming. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) The earth was barren and the farming culture was stuck in outdated, inefficient methods. But Schalk and his partners painstakingly built up the land, installing Georgia’s very first pivot irrigation system - a mechanised sprinkler that waters large fields efficiently. In just two years, they transformed hundreds of hectares of fallow land into productive fields…sharing their knowledge along the way. (SCHALK KRUGER) Actually, Georgians are very, very quick learners. And the moment we we start developed with daai centre pivot opsit, die volgende jaar dan begin julle pivots ook opsit me and the government give them cheap loans (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Things were looking up…. but only briefly. After just five years, Schalk threw in the towel, frustrated by clashes with neighbours over water and grazing rights and the rising costs of farming. (SCHALK KRUGER) We planted 200 hectares and we think we will pay for 200 hectares of water. No, we’ve got 1000 hectares. We must pay for a 1000 hectares of water. We must pay for a 1000 hectares of land tax. Even if we not use it and let that is 250,000. Every year there's more than a million rand a year that we didn’t bargain on. So we ran out of cash. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Schalk sold for a small profit and moved on. The land he developed is now in Georgian hands. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) It’s a common story among the South Africans farming here. Some, like Schalk, sold their farms and stayed in Georgia. Many returned home. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) This farm was built up using South African expertise. Some of these very farming implements and equipment being imported from there into Georgia. Its success hinging on the support given by the first generation of South African farmers that immigrated here almost 15 years ago. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Leven Akhvledini is here largely thanks to the South Africans. A lawyer by training, he’s spent the past decade farming. He’s one of several Georgian professionals moving into agriculture off the back of South African skills. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) His 110-hectare farm in a place called Sartichala produces 14 tonnes of maize per hectare. (LEVEN AKHVLEDINI) This idea of, South Africans to Georgia. I think it was successful because this focal point, what we did here is spread around and we show this success story to the neighbours, to the all the other regions and Georgians, farmers, and they start following. And, you know, they copy, copy, paste us (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Leven and many other novice Georgian farmers have learned the ins and outs from Piet Kemp, a farmer from Heilbron in the Free State. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) He’s currently overseeing thousands of hectares down the road from Leven, producing wheat, corn and cattle for a Georgian consortium. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) He says there was almost nothing here when he first arrived (PIET KEMP) The problems, think I got was in the beginning to get the infrastructure there. And I think is is now really in place. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Some people call you the South African godfather of farming in Georgia. What do you think about that? (PIET KEMP) No, I'm just a small farmer who try to help this people. And I can see what is the challenge here. And I try to take on the challenges. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Oom Piet is in his eighties and still going strong, but he doesn’t own the land he works. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Aren’t you bitter at all now that I mean, you're 81 years of age. You've spent 15 years, good years, farming in Georgia, and you still don't own your own farm? (PIET KEMP) No, I love this farm. All the farms here. I'm looking for the same as my own from South Africa. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) In 2017 the Georgian government delivered a sucker punch to the South Africans farmers who’d stuck it out; making it illegal for foreigners to own agricultural land. NICKOLAUS BAUER Did it become more difficult when they changed the law? PIET KEMP I think so I'm a little bit worried about it, but I don't talk about it. NICKOLAUS BAUER Piet was the very first South African farmer to come to Georgia 15 years ago. But with the change in agricultural laws and the growth and competitiveness of the industry, it's doubtful any more will come soon. And with numbers dwindling, the story of South African farming in this Eastern European state might be coming to an end. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Georgia is a very different place to what Piet and the other first South African farmers encountered. The current government is turning away from the West, and no longer eager to open the economy to foreign investment. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Now, it’s a place of arbitrary arrests… (NICKOLAUS BAUER) …protests and a crackdown on media freedom. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) It’s a tense atmosphere we experienced, too. When we tried to speak to protesters at the Georgian parliament, our photos were taken, and we were ordered to leave. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Hardly an ideal environment for foreigners from the tip of Africa who just want to farm. But Leven insists politics isn’t why South African farming in Georgia is declining. NICKOLAUS BAUER Why do you think that there aren't that many South African farmers still farming in Georgia, though? (LEVEN AKHVLEDINI) I think it is cultural misunderstanding also sometimes. (I think it is cultural misunderstanding also sometimes. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Whatever the reason, there are just a handful of South African farmers still in business here. Some are even being subsidized by their operations back home. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Charles Melville, from Addo in the Eastern Cape, and is one of the few South Africans still active in Georgia on his own land. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) It hasn’t been easy. CHARLES MELVILLE Pioneers get shot at. So we were pioneers and we got shot at. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Charles doesn’t believe the incentives that brought South Africans farmers here were genuine. (CHARLES MELVILLE) All of us didn't do our homework properly. And in the beginning we were sort of lied to how easy it was to acquire the land, how badly they needed us. But the government wasn't even aware of what was required. For instance, they'd say, take that piece of land in some Georgian would crawl out, the woodwork, and then you'd say, hang on, hang on. I've got a piece of paper for this from Russian Times. Luckily, I had, a fair sized fortune when I left South Africa. It's now a small fortune, (NICKOLAUS BAUER) He’s also struggled to maintain his property rights. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) The Georgian government tried to block the transfer of land he bought before the ownership law changed in 2017 and only processed the transaction when he took them to court. (CHARLES MELVILLE) Many countries make it difficult for foreigners to own agricultural land. I think the safest for any foreign is to not getting involved in local politics. You've actually got nothing to do with the local politics. Leave it to the locals to sort out. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) So you're not worried that government may in the future change the laws and take your land away from you? (CHARLES MELVILLE) No, not at all. Because, If they did that, then the rule of law would also be gone in Georgia, (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Charles has decided to keep his head down, hoping to develop the local beef industry with several hundred cattle. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) We asked the Georgian government about their stance on South African farmers and foreign land ownership, but they didn’t respond. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Agriculture now makes up 7% of the Georgian economy and the country is still importing more food than it produces. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Many South Africans have returned home, but not everybody is in a hurry to leave. Even if they aren’t farming anymore. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Schalk has settled in Tbilisi with his Georgian wife Ekatarina. EKATARINA KRUGER We joking sometimes. I say you especially come for me, not to become farmer. Maybe because to find me. (SCHALK KRUGER) I don't want to go back. I'm happy here. No, no, for me. I will not get back. I. I find my happiness here, and I will stay. Yeah. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) So would you say Georgia's your home now? (SCHALK KRUGER) Ya! Ya! (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Oom, you asked for some Bovril so I brought you some all the way from South Africa. (SCHALK KRUGER) Look dear! You know what’s this? (EKATARINA KRUGER) Of course! (SCHALK KRUGER) Black gold! Jirre! Lekker! (SCHALK KRUGER) Bovril and Georgian khachapuri loop mooi saam! (NICKOLAUS BAUER) IS dit jou ontbyt? (Is that your breakfast?) (SCHALK KRUGER) Nie onbyt! Aandete! Enige tyd van die dae! metadata.Unique Selling Point: Exclusive follow up by South African media on the South African farming community in Georgia since its beginnings 15 years ago
metadata.Summary: For nearly two decades, a community of South African farmers has carved out a life in the fertile valleys of the Republic of Georgia — a land once scarred by Soviet rule, now transformed into an unlikely home for expat agriculturalists. But the same soil that once offered new hope is now the site of rising tension, quiet dispossession, and shifting legal sands. New restrictions on foreign ownership of agricultural land, coupled with state interference in production rights, have left some farmers thriving — and others stripped of everything they’ve built. As Georgia tightens its grip on food sovereignty, Carte Blanche travels to the Caucasus to uncover the untold story of South African farmers who say they were welcomed in, only to be quietly pushed out. This story explores the rise, fall, and uncertain future of a pioneering community, caught between geopolitics, legal grey zones, and the unrelenting demands of survival.
metadata.Further information: Key Themes: The Dream: South Africans began arriving in Georgia in the early 2010s, drawn by arable land and promises of opportunity Community efforts led to commercial farms producing beef, vegetables and supporting food security in Georgia Initial government support and community acceptance The Shift: Recent laws prohibit foreign ownership of agricultural land without special government dispensation Some farmers have kept their land under complex leases or local proxies Others claim the state used water permits, sales blockades, and licensing bureaucracy to force them off The Fallout: Former farmers like Schalk Krüger describe a slow-motion “expropriation” Rising mistrust and refusal by most expats to speak publicly Growing sense of betrayal and legal limbo Tensions between Georgia’s national food strategy and individual farmers’ rights The Broader Landscape: Georgia’s positioning as a low-tax haven and crypto-friendly hub Growing South African presence not just in agriculture, but tech, medicine and financial services Mixed messages from the Georgian state — pro-investment but increasingly protectionist Echoes of South Africa’s own land reform debates playing out in reverse Visual Approach: Cinematic Rural Georgia: Drone shots of fertile farmland, machinery, and homesteads in contrast with abandoned fields and government-seized properties Testimony and Tension: Walk-and-talk interviews with farmers on their land (and those who’ve lost it), showing subtle fear, resilience, and resignation Documents and Data: Legal graphics outlining changes in Georgian agricultural law; satellite imagery of seized land; maps of Georgian-South African farming zones Contrast and Context: Scenes from Tbilisi’s crypto and forex hubs juxtaposed with remote, embattled farmsteads Emotional Layer: Intimate reflections on community, betrayal, and what it means to start again — only to be uprooted twice
